name: Affine lines in the plane
questiontext:
A linear line in the plane is a one dimensional subspace of \(R^2\) of the form \(m = Span(v)\) where \(0 \ne v \in R^2\). An affine line is a translation of a linear line; obtained by adding one constant vector \(\ell : m + w_1 = \{\alpha v + w_1 \ | \ \alpha \in R\}\). In the picture we see how we can replace \(w_1\) by a different point \(w_2\) on the same affine to obtain a new parametrization of the same line \(\ell: m+w2=\{\beta v + w_2 \ | \ \beta \in R\}\). 

Two affine lines \(\ell_1 = w_1+Span(v_1), \ell_2 = w_2 + Span(v_2)\) can be in one of three possible mutual configurations (1) Parallel, (2) Intersecting, and (3) Coincident (namely they are the same line). The following pictures demonstrate these possibilities.   

Consider the following lines 

\[\ell_1: {{CT:0}}+Span \left( {{CT:1}} \right),   \ell_2: {{CT:2}} + Span \left( {{CT:3}} \right) \]

on_true.feedback: • Yes this is the correct configuration of the two lines.

The first thing to note is that the direction vectors v1={{CT:4}} and v2={{CT:5}} are linearly independent. In the plane this means that the two lines must intersect.

For the future note that in \(R^3\) this is not the case anymore.

on_false.feedback:
The first thing to note is that the direction vectors \(v_1={{CT:1}} and v_2={{CT:3}}\) are linearly dependent. This means that the two lines are either parallel or coincident. 

Even thought the two lines do not come with the same parameterization they might still coincide. As shown in the first figure. However since we already determined that the lines are either coincident or parallel it would be enough to check one point. For example we can check if \(w_2={{CT:2}} \in \ell_1\) by solving the linear equation \(w_2 = w_1 + \alpha v_1\). Explicitly this is a system of two equations with one unknown \(\alpha\) 

\[{{CT:2}} = {{CT:0}} + \alpha {{CT:1}} \]

on_true.feedback: Since this equation has a solution we deduce that \(w_2 \in \ell_1\) and hence the two lines are coincident.

on_false.feedback: Since this equation does not have a solution we deduce that \(w_2 \not \in \ell_1\) and hence the two lines are parallel but not coincident.

on_true.feedback: • You calculated the distance between the lines correctly.

on_false.feedback: • You didn't calculate the distance between the lines correctly.

on_true.feedback: Since the two lines are intersecting, the distance between them must be zero.
Since the two lines coincide the distance between them must be zero.

on_false.feedback:
One way to do this is as follows. Since the two lines are parallel we can find a vector that is orthogonal to the directions of both lines. This can be done for example by applying rotation by 90 degrees to \(v_1\) as follows:

\[o = {{CT:6}} {{CT:1}} = {{CT:7}}\]

Now as the following picture shows, projecting \(w_2-w_1\) on the orthogonal direction gives a vector whose length is just the distance between the two lines. 

\[dist = \left| \left| \frac{ (w_2-w_1)\cdot o}{o \cdot o} o \right| \right| = {{CT:8}}\]
